content: Maternal health care refers to the medical and supportive care provided to women before conception, during pregnancy, and after childbirth. Preconception care aims to promote health, screen for potential risks, and implement interventions for women of reproductive age to minimize factors that could negatively impact future pregnancies. Prenatal care involves comprehensive medical attention and self-care throughout pregnancy. Women who initiate prenatal care early in their pregnancies tend to have better birth outcomes compared to those who receive little or no care. Postnatal care focuses on recovery from childbirth, addressing concerns about newborn care, ensuring proper nutrition, supporting breastfeeding, and planning for future family needs. A significant issue is that many women, particularly in developing countries, lack access to essential healthcare and sexual health education. In these regions, complications related to pregnancy and childbirth are the leading causes of death among women of reproductive age. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), over 585,000 women die annually from such causes, equating to more than one death per minute. Less than 1% of these deaths occur in developed countries, highlighting the preventable nature of these fatalities if adequate resources and services were available. Pregnancy, childbirth, and the postpartum period can present sudden and severe complications for any woman. While high-quality healthcare has made maternal deaths rare in developed nations, these complications often prove fatal in developing countries. Women in these regions die during childbirth at rates that are 100 times or more higher than those in developed nations. Access to emergency obstetric care, which is critical for saving lives, is not prioritized in many developing areas. Barriers to healthcare include long distances to medical facilities, high costs (including fees, transportation, medications, and supplies), competing demands on women’s time, and a lack of decision-making power within families. Additionally, poor-quality healthcare services and mistreatment by providers deter some women from seeking care. The World Health Report of 2004 identified poor maternal health conditions as the fourth leading cause of death among women, following HIV/AIDS, malaria, and tuberculosis. A staggering 99% of maternal deaths occur in low-income countries. In developed nations, the risk of dying during pregnancy or childbirth is 1 in 4,000, whereas in Sub-Saharan Africa, the risk is 1 in 16. Maternal health issues also account for nearly 20% of the total disease burden for women in developing countries. Alarmingly, almost half of all births in these regions occur without the assistance of a skilled healthcare provider, with the proportion being even higher in South Asia. To address these challenges, the World Bank estimates that an annual investment of $3 per person could provide basic family planning, maternal, and neonatal healthcare in developing countries. Numerous non-profit organizations are working to educate the public and improve access to emergency obstetric care. Essential services include routine maternal care for all pregnancies, skilled attendance (by a midwife or doctor) during childbirth, emergency treatment for complications, postpartum family planning, and basic neonatal care. Educating women and their communities about the importance of maternal health is crucial, as is empowering women to make healthcare decisions and seek medical attention. Even six years of education for girls can significantly improve maternal health outcomes. Research into the social and psychological factors affecting maternal health, as well as the development and evaluation of interventions for complex issues (e.g., behavioral, social, biological, and cultural challenges), is also vital. Progress in maternal health varies by region. According to the Millennium Development Goals (MDG), regions such as Sub-Saharan Africa, Southeastern Asia, Southern Asia, and Oceania have shown significant improvements. However, Northern Africa, Western Asia, and Latin America and the Caribbean are progressing more slowly. Eastern Asia, Europe (Commonwealth of Independent States), and Asia (Commonwealth of Independent States) have shown little to no progress, with some areas even regressing. Despite notable advancements in maternal health over the past century, the last decade has seen a slower rate of improvement in maternal mortality and morbidity, particularly in Latin America and the Caribbean. Currently, only about 17% of countries are on track to meet the MDG targets for maternal health.
